canonicalExplanation.summary: A good feature branch is **short-lived and focused**. Start it from an **up-to-date base** (fetch first, then branch from `origin/main`). Keep it to **one concern**, with small reviewable commits. Before asking for review, **check the base and tip**: `git log --oneline main..feature` should list only your commits. If main has moved on, bring those changes in (merge or rebase) and re-test. Branches don't prevent conflicts by themselves; staying small and short does. Long-lived branches drift away from main and make integration painful.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner starts a dark-mode feature branch from their local main, which hasn't been updated in two weeks. Three weeks later their pull request shows 40 commits, including other people's old work, and conflicts everywhere. A short feature branch begins from current main, contains one tested concern, and opens a review before merging back. In this lesson you'll complete an isolated feature branch and verify the base and tip before integration.

```predict
{"question": "You create a branch from a local main you haven't updated in weeks. Is it based on the latest main?", "options": ["Yes, branches always start from the newest main", "No: it starts from whatever your local main points to"], "answer": 1, "why": "Fetch first and branch from origin/main to start from the real latest."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Commits and history**, **Branches as movable refs** and **Commit messages and scope**.

sections.heading: The workflow rule: fresh base, one concern, verify
sections.body:
```bash
git fetch origin
git switch -c feature/dark-mode origin/main   # start from the real latest main.

# work in small commits...
git commit -m "Add theme toggle button"
git commit -m "Persist theme choice in localStorage"

git fetch origin
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD           # only my commits?
git merge-base HEAD origin/main               # where did I branch from?
npm test                                      # re-test on the current base.
git push -u origin feature/dark-mode          # then open a review.
```

| Healthy branch | Warning sign |
|---|---|
| days old. | weeks or months old. |
| one concern. | "feature + refactor + fixes". |
| main..HEAD lists only your commits. | other people's commits appear. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "What does main..HEAD mean in git log?", "answer": "Commits reachable from HEAD but not from main: exactly what your branch adds. If that list surprises you, your base is wrong."}
```

sections.heading: Scope creep

includes: Start branches from a freshly fetched base and keep them to one concern.
Verify base and tip with main..HEAD and merge-base, and re-test before review.

outcomes: Complete an isolated feature branch and verify the base and tip before integration.

examples.title: The dark-mode toggle branch
examples.situation: A short feature branch begins from current main, contains one tested concern, and opens a review before merging back.
walkthrough: **Begins from current main:** git fetch then git switch -c feature/dark-mode origin/main.
**Contains one tested concern:** two small commits for the toggle and persistence; tests pass.
**Opens a review before merging back:** git log origin/main..HEAD shows just those two commits, so the review will be small.
examples.result: The review is quick, the merge is clean, and the branch is deleted within days.

examples.title: The branch that lived for a month
examples.situation: A branch adds search, refactors the API client and fixes two bugs over five weeks. The review stalls at 3,000 lines.
walkthrough: Too many concerns and too much drift from main.
Split: land the bug fixes first, then the refactor, then search.
Bring main in often so conflicts stay small.
examples.result: Three reviewable branches merge in a week instead of one that never does.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Creating many branches automatically prevents conflicts and guarantees changes are based on the latest target.
misconceptions.correction: A branch starts wherever you create it, and conflicts come from overlapping edits over time. Fresh bases, small scope and short lifetimes are what reduce conflicts.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what was the branch actually based on?

analogy.example: A feature branch is like **borrowing a library book**: take the current edition (fresh base), use it for one purpose, and return it quickly. Keep it for months and the library has moved on, with a new edition your notes don't match.
limitations: Library books don't change; main does, every day.
You can bring in the new edition's changes (merge or rebase) before returning.

steps.explanation: The short feature branch begins from current main.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo with a remote, create a feature branch from origin/main, make two commits, then show main..HEAD and the merge-base. Explain what each output proves.
scaffold: A bare local repo can be the remote.

farTransfer.prompt: Simulate drift: make a feature branch, then advance main with a teammate's commit. Update your branch with the new main, re-run tests, and show that main..HEAD still lists only your commits.
scaffold: git merge origin/main or git rebase origin/main.
expectedEvidence: Your commits are still the only additions.

remediation.explanation: Before starting: **fetch, and branch from origin/main**. Before review: **main..HEAD shows only my commits, tests pass on the current base.**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The branch that lived for a month".

recap.summary: To complete an isolated feature branch, fetch and start from the current target, keep one tested concern in small commits, verify with main..HEAD and merge-base that the base and tip are what you expect, update and re-test if main moved, and open a review quickly.
